cues.text: In 1345, thieves broke into the small Collegiate Church of All Saints in the village of Wawel, just outside Kraków , and made off with a golden monstrance from the tabernacle, believing they had found a genuine treasure.
Once safely away from the church, the thieves examined their prize more closely and realized the monstrance was not the valuable gold they had assumed.
Disappointed, they discarded it, along with the several consecrated Hosts it still held, into a nearby marsh and fled.
That night, a mysterious light began rising from the spot in the marsh where the monstrance had been thrown, bright enough to be seen for several kilometers.
Frightened villagers who investigated could find nothing, but reported the strange flashes to the Bishop of Kraków.
He called for three days of fasting and prayer among the faithful before acting.
On the third day, the bishop led a procession to the section of marsh where the lights had appeared.
There, the monstrance was recovered, with the consecrated Hosts inside clean and undamaged despite being buried in mud.
The lights were never seen again after that day.

In thanksgiving, King Casimir III the Great of Poland ordered a church built on the site and dedicated to Corpus Christi, still standing in Kraków today, its walls holding paintings and documents recording the episode.

The feast of Corpus Christi has been celebrated there with particular solemnity ever since, and the church itself became, in later centuries, associated with the parish where a young Karol Wojtyła would one day celebrate his own first Mass nearby.
